items.correct_answer: Rubric and model response. This essay is not auto-scored and has no single correct answer: a response taking the opposite position can score just as well if it is argued as well. Score your own response against this rubric, 0 to 2 points on each line. (1) Position: a clear position stated early and held throughout. (2) Reasons and examples: two or three reasons, each developed with a specific example. (3) Counterargument: the strongest opposing view engaged and answered, not ignored. (4) Organisation and language: clear paragraph structure, precise vocabulary and varied sentences. Model response sketch (one defensible position, not the only one): basic research has no obvious application by definition, yet its payoffs arrive decades later in unexpected places: the mathematics of number theory now secures online payments, and curiosity-driven biology produced the tools behind modern vaccines. Leaving such work to markets alone would starve it, since no firm can capture returns it cannot foresee. Governments should therefore fund it, judging proposals on the quality of the question rather than on a promised product, while requiring open publication so the public that pays can use the results.
items.explanation: This item is an essay-scoring task, not a keyed question. There is no single correct answer: the opposite position, that governments should fund only research with obvious practical application, can score equally well if it is argued as well. Judge your response against the rubric in the model response: a clear position held throughout, reasons each developed with a specific example, the strongest objection answered, and clear organisation with precise vocabulary. The model sketch shows one defensible position; it is an example of good structure, not the answer to copy. The engine does not auto-score essays: it records the response and shows this rubric and model sketch for comparison.
items.question: Write a response to the following issue. Governments should fund basic scientific research even when it has no obvious practical application. Take a clear position and support it with reasons and examples. Consider the strongest objection to your view and explain why it does not overturn your position.

items.explanation: The debate had every member speaking at length and the chair unable to close the meeting, so it was protracted, meaning long drawn out, rather than brisk, meaning short and businesslike. The minutes recording far more pages than any previous meeting confirms the length. Cursory means hasty, which contradicts speaking at length, and muted and lively do not describe a debate that ran on.
items.question: Choose the set of words that best completes the sentence. The committee's debate was (i)______ rather than (ii)______, with every member speaking at length, the chair unable to bring the meeting to a close, and the minutes recording (iii)______ more pages than any previous meeting.

items.explanation: The two blanks must be filled jointly. 'It celebrated the general's victories' requires generous, unstinting praise, which fits lavish, effusive and generous, but rules out restrained in the fourth option. 'Holding him responsible for the campaign's failures' requires criticism that does not soften the blame, which fits only unsparing: sparing in the first option and merciful in the third option both soften it, lenient in the fifth option softens it, and severe in the fourth option describes harshness rather than refusal to spare. Only the second option fits both clauses: lavish praise and unsparing criticism.
items.question: Choose the pair of words that best completes the sentence. The biographer's account was ______ in its praise and ______ in its criticism: it celebrated the general's victories while holding him responsible for the campaign's failures.

items.explanation: The author's argument has two halves: anchoring depends on a sustained record of keeping promises, and credibility is lost quickly and remembered long. Finding (i) of option C supports the first half, since households credit years of kept promises rather than any one announcement, and finding (ii) supports the second half, since expectations stayed unanchored for a decade after a single year of high inflation. Option A supports the single announcement view the author rejects. Option B contradicts the author on frequent target changes. Option D is irrelevant on both halves. Option E pairs a finding against the author with one for the author, so the pair does not strengthen the argument as a whole.
options: (i) Households form expectations mainly from the central bank's most recent announcement. (ii) Firms set prices by copying competitors.
(i) In countries where central banks changed targets frequently, expectations stayed low and stable. (ii) Central banks announce decisions monthly.

(i) Households interviewed after a decade of low inflation said they expected low inflation mainly because the bank had kept its promises year after year. (ii) After a central bank tolerated high inflation for a year, expectations stayed unanchored for a decade even after prices stabilised.
(i) Firms set prices by copying competitors. (ii) Central banks announce decisions monthly.
(i) Households form expectations from the most recent announcement. (ii) After high inflation, expectations stayed unanchored for a decade.
items.passage: Economists pay close attention to what people expect inflation to be, because expectations can become self-fulfilling. If workers expect prices to rise by five percent, they demand wage rises of five percent; firms, facing higher wage bills, raise their own prices by five percent, and the expectation is confirmed. Central banks therefore try to anchor expectations, convincing the public that inflation will remain low and stable. The difficulty is that credibility is earned slowly and lost quickly. A central bank that tolerates high inflation for a year may find expectations unanchored for a decade, since households remember the episode long after prices have stabilised. Anchoring expectations is thus less about any single interest-rate decision than about a sustained record of keeping promises.
items.question: Which of the following pairs of findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?

items.explanation: Step 1: trace the mechanism the passage gives. Workers who expect prices to rise demand wage rises; firms facing higher wage bills raise their own prices, and the expectation is confirmed. Step 2: remove the wage link and the chain breaks at that step: the expectation can no longer reach prices through wage demands. The other options ignore the chain: firms raise prices because wage bills rise, not independently, and nothing in the passage says expectations would act directly or vanish if workers stopped demanding.
options: continue unchanged, since firms set prices independently of wages
break at the wage link, since the expectation reaches prices through wage demands
strengthen, since expectations would then act directly on prices
vanish, since expectations would no longer exist
reverse, since firms would cut prices instead

Every other pair contains a false claim: anchoring is less about any single interest-rate decision than about a sustained record, workers demand rises matching expected inflation rather than current inflation, households remember the episode long after prices stabilise, and credibility is earned slowly and lost quickly.
options: (i) Expectations can become self-fulfilling. (ii) Anchoring expectations depends mainly on a single sharp rise in interest rates.

(i) Expectations can become self-fulfilling because workers demand wage rises matching expected inflation. (ii) A central bank that tolerates high inflation for a year may find expectations unanchored for a decade.
(i) Central banks anchor expectations by promising high inflation. (ii) Credibility is earned quickly and lost slowly.

items.explanation: Step 1: test statement I. The shopkeepers feared the ban would cut passing trade, but footfall rose afterwards and several shops extended their opening hours into the evening, which only makes sense if trade had improved, so they came to regard the ban as a success. Step 2: test statement II. The walkers expected the promenade to grow quieter without traffic, but found it crowded, and many began walking at dawn before the crowds arrived, which only makes sense if the ban had failed their hope for quiet, so they came to regard it as a failure. Step 3: test statement III. The council introduced the ban to reduce collisions and pointed to the fall in accidents as its measure of success, so footfall is the shopkeepers' evidence, not the council's, and III is false. Only I and II survive. The passage never states any group's verdict outright; each must be inferred from that group's prior expectation plus its subsequent reaction.
items.passage: When the council barred cars from the seafront promenade, the same change was read in opposite ways by the people it affected. The shopkeepers along the front had feared the ban would cut passing trade, since fewer cars would mean fewer visitors stopping on impulse. In the months after the ban, footfall along the promenade rose, and several shops extended their opening hours into the evening. The regular walkers had expected the promenade to become quieter without traffic, and instead found it crowded with strollers and street performers; many of them began walking at dawn, before the crowds arrived. The council itself had introduced the ban to reduce collisions between cars and pedestrians, and its reports pointed to the fall in accidents as the measure of whether the ban had worked.
items.question: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would agree with which of the following? Consider the statements below. I. The shopkeepers came to regard the ban as a success, since footfall rose and shops stayed open longer. II. The regular walkers came to regard the ban as a failure, since it crowded the promenade they had hoped would grow quieter. III. The council regarded the ban as a success because footfall along the promenade rose. Select the option that lists all and only the statements the author would agree with.

items.explanation: Step 1: hold the two facts the passage keeps apart. Glass is strange in its properties, transparent though made from sand, solid yet with atoms arranged like a liquid's, and that strangeness does not change. Step 2: set the uses against the properties. Glass moved from stained-glass windows and the vessels of the wealthy, through flat-glass windows in ordinary homes, to lenses, microscopes, telescopes and fibre-optic strands, ending as a screen in every pocket. The uses changed completely while the properties stayed strange, so the spread shows uses changing more radically than properties. Industrial production changed who could afford glass, not how strange it is, and flat glass, not fibre optics, put windows in ordinary homes.
options: a material's uses can change more radically than its properties
industrial production made glass less strange as a material
lenses mattered less than windows in the history of glass
glass stopped being a luxury because it became transparent
fibre optics made glass common in ordinary homes

Each other option names one group's strand, but only the different judgements of the same ban cover the whole passage.
options: the history of the seafront promenade

the profits of shops along the promenade

items.explanation: Step 1: the median of an even count of numbers is the average of the two middle numbers, so x is (47 + 53) / 2 = 50, not 47 or 53. Step 2: the sum of the five numbers is 41 + 47 + 53 + 59 + 50 = 250, and 250 / 5 = 50. Step 3: Quantity A is 50 and Quantity B is 50, so the quantities are equal. The trap is taking x to be 47, which gives an average of 49.4, or 53, which gives 50.6; both come from forgetting that a median of four numbers is an average, not one of the numbers.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

Quantity A: Average of 41, 47, 53, 59 and x, where x is the median of 41, 47, 53 and 59

Compare the two quantities.

items.explanation: Step 1: the integers from 10 to 20 inclusive are 11 numbers symmetric around 15, so their sum is 11 x 15 = 165. Step 2: removing 20 and adding 9 changes the sum to 165 - 20 + 9 = 154, while the count stays 11, so the new average is 154 / 11 = 14. Step 3: 14 is less than 15, so Quantity B is greater. The trap is assuming one removal and one addition cancel out; they do not, because 20 is above the mean and 9 is below it, and the swap pulls the mean down by 1. Checking the endpoints matters: the removed number and the added number sit on opposite sides of the mean.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
items.question:
Quantity A: Average of all integers from 10 to 20 inclusive after the integer 20 is removed and the integer 9 is added
Quantity B: 15
Compare the two quantities.

items.explanation: Step 1: write the final price as a product. The two rises multiply the price by (1 + p/100) x (1 + q/100) = 1 + (p + q)/100 + pq/10000. Step 2: use the sum. Since p + q = 30, this is 1.30 + pq/10000. Step 3: use the positivity. Both p and q are positive, so pq is positive and the final price is always above 130% of the original, whatever the split between p and q. With p = 10 and q = 20 the final price is 132%, and with p = 1 and q = 29 it is 130.29%. Quantity A is greater. The trap is to add the percentages and conclude the quantities are equal, which ignores the compounding term pq/10000.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
items.question:
A price is raised by p% and then by q%, where p + q = 30 and both p and q are positive.
Quantity A: The final price as a percentage of the original price
Quantity B: 130%
Compare the two quantities.

items.explanation: Step 1: since x and y are positive and sum to 1, each of them lies strictly between 0 and 1. Step 2: for any number t strictly between 0 and 1, the square root of t is greater than t, and t squared is less than t. So Quantity A is greater than x + y, which is 1, while Quantity B is less than x + y, which is 1. Step 3: therefore Quantity A is greater than 1 and Quantity B is less than 1, so Quantity A is greater. Check with values: x = y = 1/2 gives Quantity A about 1.414 and Quantity B 0.5, and at the extreme x = 0.01, y = 0.99, Quantity A is about 1.095 and Quantity B is about 0.980, so the direction holds at the extremes. The trap is testing a single pair of values and guessing from it, or ignoring the sum constraint and treating x and y as free.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
items.question:
x and y are positive numbers with x + y = 1.
Quantity A: the square root of x plus the square root of y
Quantity B: x squared plus y squared
Compare the two quantities.

items.explanation: Step 1: the midpoint halves CD, so the horizontal distance from A to E is half of 12, which is 6. Step 2: AE is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 6 (horizontal) and 8 (the side BC, vertical). Step 3: by Pythagoras, AE is the square root of 36 + 64 = 100, which is 10. The trap is adding the legs, 6 + 8 = 14, or using the full width 12 instead of the halved width, which gives the square root of 208. The midpoint is the whole item: without halving, there is no 6-8-10 triple to find.
items.question: ABCD is a rectangle with AB = 12 and BC = 8. E is the midpoint of CD. What is the length of AE?

items.explanation: Step 1: work out what the first sequence does. Increasing by 25% and then decreasing by 20% multiplies a number by 1.25 x 0.8 = 1, so the first original number is 600 itself. Step 2: work out what the second sequence does. Decreasing by 20% and then increasing by 25% multiplies by 0.8 x 1.25 = 1, the same product, so the second original number is also 600. The two changes commute: multiplication does not care about the order. Step 3: the difference between the two original numbers is 600 - 600 = 0. The trap is to assume that reversing the order changes the outcome and to compute a spurious difference; checking either sequence alone shows the net effect is no change at all.
items.question: A number is increased by 25% and then decreased by 20%. The result is 600. A second number is decreased by 20% and then increased by 25%. The result is also 600. What is the difference between the two original numbers?

items.explanation: The average of three numbers is 74, so their total is 222. Two of them are 62 and 74, so the third is 222 minus 136, which is 86. Doubling the third gives 172, and adding a fourth number equal to the original third gives 86. The four numbers are 62, 74, 172 and 86, totalling 394, and 394 divided by 4 is 98.5. The trap is to average the original three numbers instead of the new set, or to forget the doubling.
items.question: The average of three numbers is 74. Two of the numbers are 62 and 74. The third number is then doubled, and a fourth number, equal to the original third number, is added. What is the new average of the four numbers?

items.explanation: Step 1: the five numbers total 5 x 60 = 300, so the fifth number is 300 - 52 - 58 - 64 - 70 = 56. Step 2: increasing it by 10 makes it 66, so the new total is 300 + 10 = 310. Step 3: the new average is 310 / 5 = 62. The trap is answering 66, which is the new fifth number itself, not the new average; a second trap is adding 10 to the average to get 70, which is not listed, or adding 10 / 5 = 2 to 60, which does give 62 but only if the candidate sees why the increase is spread across all five numbers.
items.question: The average of five numbers is 60. Four of the numbers are 52, 58, 64 and 70. The fifth number is then increased by 10. What is the new average of the five numbers?

items.explanation: Statement I is true: (5/10) x (4/9) = 2/9. Statement II is true: after a blue ball is removed, 5 red balls remain out of 9, so the conditional probability is 5/9, not the unconditional 1/2. Statement III is false: both red has probability 2/9 and both blue also 2/9, so the same-colour probability is 4/9, not 1/2. Only I and II are true.
items.question: A bag contains 5 red balls and 5 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after another without replacement. Consider the statements below. I. The probability that both balls are red is 2/9. II. The probability that the second ball drawn is red, given that the first ball drawn is blue, is 5/9. III. The probability that the two balls are of the same colour is 1/2. Select the option that lists all and only the true statements.

items.explanation: Step 1: the neither count is largest when the union is smallest, since neither is 60 minus the union. Step 2: the union is smallest when the overlap is largest. The overlap cannot exceed the smaller set, 25 football players, so the smallest possible union is 28, with every football player also playing cricket. Step 3: the greatest possible neither count is therefore 60 - 28 = 32. The traps are 7, from assuming no overlap at all, which gives the smallest neither count rather than the largest, and 35, from subtracting only the football total. The bound is attainable: with all 25 football players inside the cricket set, 28 play at least one game and 32 play neither.
items.question: In a group of 60 students, 28 play cricket and 25 play football. What is the greatest possible number who play neither game?

items.explanation: Step 1: count by place, not by listing. In the units place, 7 appears once in every ten numbers, so 40 times in 1 to 400. Step 2: in the tens place, 7 appears in the blocks 70-79, 170-179, 270-279 and 370-379, which is 10 x 4 = 40 times. Step 3: in the hundreds place, 7 never appears, because the range stops at 400 and there is no 700s block. The total is 40 + 40 = 80. The predictable wrong answers are 70 (forgetting the 370-379 block) and 120 (counting a 700s block that does not exist). There are no options to eliminate, so the decomposition and the boundary at 400 are the whole item.
items.question: In writing all of the integers from 1 to 400 inclusive, how many times is the digit 7 used?

items.explanation: Step 1: powers of 3 leave remainders 3, 4, 2, 1 in a cycle of 4 when divided by 5, and 50 leaves remainder 2 on division by 4, so 3^50 leaves remainder 4. Step 2: powers of 2 leave remainders 2, 4, 3, 1 in a cycle of 4, and 50 again leaves remainder 2, so 2^50 also leaves remainder 4. Step 3: the sum leaves remainder 4 + 4 = 8, and 8 divided by 5 leaves remainder 3. The trap is adding the bases first, or forgetting to reduce the summed remainder modulo 5 a second time, which gives 8 instead of 3.
items.question: What is the remainder when 3^50 + 2^50 is divided by 5?

items.explanation: Step 1: the opening metaphor, slippery ground, states the historian's position, and the rest of the sentence restates it as a list of evidence, with especially marking the restatement. Step 2: the blank needs a word for a position, not a method, so precarious fits: her footing is insecure. Step 3: eliminate the method words. Meticulous describes how carefully she works, ingenious describes how cleverly, and neither describes her position; laudable and crucial praise the work rather than the ground it stands on. The trap is matching a positive word to a historian who is working hard, when the sentence is about how insecure her evidence is.
items.question: Choose the word that best completes the sentence. A historian on slippery ground with her sources is ______: the archives are fragmentary, the chronicles contradict one another, and, especially, the few surviving letters are undated.

items.explanation: Step 1, the control comparison: the treated group's fever fell, but the untreated group's fever fell within a day as well, so the fall cannot be credited to the remedy. The first clause alone tempts "effective", but combined with the control clause it shows the remedy did nothing to the fever, so blank (i) is ineffective. Step 2, scope, symptom versus cure: recovery time, not the fever's fall, is the measure that bears on whether the remedy cures the illness, and no patient taking it recovered sooner, so blank (ii) is useless. "Unproven" would fit a trial that had never measured recovery, but this trial measured it in every patient and found no difference at all, which is positive evidence of no effect, not an absence of evidence. Step 3, the conceptual step, a perspective-relative judgment: the physicians' decision must be judged by the evidence they had, not by the full trial outcome. They had seen only the treated-group results, in which every fever fell, so prescribing on that evidence was understandable, even though the remedy itself is ineffective; "inexcusable" condemns them for knowledge they did not have. Only the fifth option survives all three blanks: the first and third options fail blank (i), the second fails blank (ii), and the fourth fails blank (iii).
items.question: Choose the set of words that best completes the sentence. In the trial, the fever of every patient given the new remedy fell within a day; the fever of patients given nothing fell within a day as well, and no patient taking the remedy recovered sooner than a patient given nothing. The physicians, who had seen only the results for patients given the remedy, prescribed it widely. The remedy was (i)______ against the fever and (ii)______ against the illness, and the physicians' decision to prescribe it was (iii)______.

The speaker began (i)______, grew (ii)______ once challenged, and ended (iii)______: the audience that had nearly drifted away during his opening leaned forward when he answered his critics, and those who leaned forward stayed to applaud him at the end.

items.explanation: Step 1: blank (i). The report praised record earnings, so its account of the profits was favourable, not dismissive. Step 2: blank (ii). It described unsafe workshops, so its account of the workers' conditions was critical; sympathetic would excuse the conditions rather than condemn them. Step 3: blank (iii). The final judgement cannot be settled from either chapter alone: it must weigh praised earnings against unsafe workshops, and it concludes that a business cannot be called successful, so the judgement is unsparing, not approving. The new option that differs only in blank (iii) fails at that last step, and the option that is dismissive and sympathetic fails at the first two steps. items.explanation: The lecture covered in an hour what a textbook takes a chapter to explain, and nothing essential had been left out, so it was both brief and complete. Succinct and terse both mean brief and to the point, and both fit a lecture that lost nothing essential. Prolix, diffuse and rambling all mean wordy, which contradicts the hour-versus-chapter contrast. Compressed fits the brevity but cryptic means obscure, which contradicts students passing without the textbook.
items.question: Select the pair of answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. The professor's lecture was ______, covering in an hour what a textbook takes a chapter to explain, and the students who attended it passed the exam without opening the textbook, because nothing essential had been left out.

items.explanation: Unstinting means generous and without holding back, which fits praise that commends the research's depth and range, and unconvincing means failing to persuade, which fits an argument the review found weak, with yet marking the contrast between the two judgements. Grudging and sparing both contradict commending the research's depth and range. Compelling contradicts finding the argument weak, since a compelling argument persuades.
items.question: Choose the pair of words that best completes the sentence. The review was (i)______ in its praise of the book's research, commending its depth and range, yet it found the book's central argument (ii)______.

items.explanation: Step 1: the complaint is that the report's recommendations contradict each other, so readers cannot pin the report to one meaning. That forces a word meaning open to more than one interpretation, which is equivocal and ambiguous. Step 2: reject meticulous and scrupulous. They are genuine synonyms, and the stem's phrase carefully drafted seems to invite them, but they describe the report's care, while the complaint is that its recommendations cannot be pinned down. Step 3: reject prolix and verbose. They are about length, and the rewritten stem says nothing about length or repeated evidence, so the wordiness pair has no support at all. Step 4: reject tendentious and biased, which are about motive, and nothing in the stem suggests the report favours one side. The mixed pair equivocal and meticulous is not a synonym pair. The trap is matching carefully drafted to meticulous instead of following the contradiction clue.
items.question: Select the pair of answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. The committee's report was carefully drafted but oddly _______, its recommendations pulling in opposite directions on the same page, so that even sympathetic readers could not say whether it was urging caution or action.

items.explanation: Step 1: the correct pair must satisfy both halves of the sentence at once: the praise commends the effort, and it says nothing about the result. Guarded and qualified do both, praising with reserve. Step 2: test the half-fitting pairs. Warm and generous fit the first half, commending the effort, but they praise without the reserve the second half requires. Tepid and lukewarm fit the second half, saying little, but they contradict the commendation in the first half. Step 3: effusive and lavish are genuine synonyms that fit praise in general, but they contradict the restraint the sentence describes, and guarded and lavish is not a synonym pair. The item is hard because two decoy pairs each fit exactly one half of the sentence.
items.question: Select the pair of answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. The speaker was ______ in her praise, commending the effort while saying nothing about the result.

items.explanation: Step 1: combine the alignment sentence with the geography sentence. When Sun, Moon and Earth align, their pulls combine to produce especially high spring tides. Step 2: in a narrow bay the tidal range can be many times greater than in the open ocean, so the bay multiplies whatever tide the alignment produces. Step 3: the largest tides therefore need both conditions together, alignment and amplification. The trap is the last option: amplification is real, but when Sun and Moon pull at right angles the tides are neap, the smallest, so amplifying a small tide still gives a small tide. It is true on one clause and false on the conjunction, which is the signature hard-RC trap.
options: the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and the bay is wide

items.passage: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, and their main cause is the Moon's gravity. The Moon pulls most strongly on the ocean facing it, creating a bulge of water, and a second bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth, where the pull is weakest and inertia dominates. As the Earth rotates through these bulges, most coasts experience two high tides and two low tides each day. The Sun also affects tides, and when Sun, Moon and Earth align, their pulls combine to produce especially high spring tides. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, the tides are at their smallest, the neap tides. Local geography then modifies the pattern: in a narrow bay, the tidal range can be many times greater than in the open ocean.

items.passage: A seed bank is a library of the world's crops, stored as seeds in cold, dry vaults. Its purpose is insurance: if a disease wipes out a variety in the field, or a war destroys a region's farming, the seeds can be drawn on to start again. The best-known vault, on a Norwegian island in the Arctic, holds over a million samples, kept frozen in permafrost. Yet a seed bank is not a substitute for farming the varieties it stores. Seeds kept in cold storage do not evolve with changing pests and climates, while varieties grown in fields continue to adapt. Conservationists therefore argue that seed banks must be paired with living collections: farms and gardens where old varieties are still grown, still changing, and still available to breeders.

Quantity A against Quantity B is 1/(1 + x) against 1 - x/2, which is 2 against (2 - x)(1 + x). Step 2: expand the right side. (2 - x)(1 + x) = 2 + x - x squared, which exceeds 2 whenever x - x squared is positive. Step 3: read the sign. For 0 < x < 1, x(1 - x) is positive, so (2 - x)(1 + x) is greater than 2 and Quantity B is greater. Check with x = 1/2: Quantity A is 2/3, about 0.667, and Quantity B is 3/4, about 0.75. items.explanation: Step 1: work out each scheme as a function of P. After the two discounts Scheme A stands at 0.75 x 0.8 = 0.6P, and the Rs 50 coupon applies only when 0.6P is at least 300, that is, when P is at least 500. Scheme B stands at 0.55P after its discount, and the 5% charge brings it to 0.55 x 1.05 = 0.5775P. Step 2: compare below the threshold. When P is below 500 there is no coupon, so Scheme A costs 0.6P against Scheme B at 0.5775P, and Scheme B is cheaper. Step 3: compare at and above the threshold. With the coupon Scheme A costs 0.6P - 50, which beats 0.5775P whenever 0.0225P is below 50, that is, whenever P is below about 2222, which holds for every price in the given range. Check the boundary: at P = 500 Scheme A costs 250 and Scheme B costs 288.75, while at P = 499 Scheme A costs 299.40 and Scheme B costs 288.17. So Scheme A is cheaper exactly when the marked price is Rs 500 or more. The trap is to apply the coupon at every price, which makes Scheme A look cheaper throughout, or to ignore it, which makes Scheme B look cheaper throughout.

items.explanation: Step 1: use the complement. The probability of at least one head in n tosses is 1 minus the probability of no heads, which is 1 - (1/2)^n. Step 2: test n = 3. The probability of no heads is 1/8 = 0.125, so the probability of at least one head is 0.875, which does not exceed 0.9. Step 3: test n = 4. The probability of no heads is 1/16 = 0.0625, so the probability of at least one head is 0.9375, which does exceed 0.9. The answer is therefore 4. The trap is answering 3, which is only just short, or 5, which overshoots without checking whether 4 already works. The item asks for a threshold n, not a probability, so the candidate must test the boundary.

items.explanation: Write the integer as 100a + 10b + c, with a from 1 to 9 and b and c from 0 to 9. Reversing the digits gives 100c + 10b + a, so the sum of the two numbers is 101(a + c) + 20b. Step 1, change of representation: work modulo 11, where 101 leaves remainder 2 and 20 leaves remainder 9, which is the same as minus 2, so the sum is divisible by 11 exactly when 2(a + c) minus 2b is a multiple of 11, that is, when a + c and b leave the same remainder on division by 11. Step 2, the case split: a + c ranges from 1 to 18 and b from 0 to 9, so a + c minus b ranges from minus 8 to 18, and the only multiples of 11 it can equal are 0 and 11. Step 3, count each case with the asymmetric digit ranges: a + c equal to b gives 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9, or 45, numbers, since for each b from 1 to 9 there are b choices of a from 1 to b, and b equal to 0 gives none, since a is at least 1. For a + c equal to b + 11, the sums 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 give 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 pairs, or 36 numbers, since a is at least 1 and c at most 9. The total is 45 + 36, or 81. The trap is to count only the a + c equal to b case and answer 45, or to forget that a cannot be zero and overcount the boundary cases. Exhaustive enumeration of all three-digit numbers confirms 81.
